evaluation.positioning_hook: A small-town school custodian and a local podcast host uncover a buried trafficking network running through the church and police, forcing them to choose between exposure and survival.

audience_appeal_marketability.reasoning: The missing-girl / corrupt-institution engine is immediately legible and commercially familiar, with a clean promise of danger, conspiracy, and moral urgency. It plays to adult thriller audiences, though the regional specificity and procedural texture make it more targeted than four-quadrant.

conceptual_hook_clarity.reasoning: The hook lands fast: a custodian and a podcast host find a pattern behind a runaway case, then discover the church and police are entangled in it. The act-one escalation is clear and the hidden-system reveal gives the premise a strong, easy-to-pitch engine.

character_appeal_and_long_term_potential.reasoning: Ralph’s quiet, observant custodian persona gives the script a distinctive center, and Savannah has enough drive and skepticism to feel like a real counterweight. They function well together, though the supporting cast is more functional than deeply individualized.

creative_originality_and_boldness.reasoning: The choice to anchor the story around a school custodian and a podcast investigator is fresh, and the Skook-specific setting gives it identity. The underlying conspiracy-thriller architecture is familiar, so the originality comes more from packaging than from form.

narrative_momentum_engagement.reasoning: The script moves with purpose from the football-field cold open to the church tunnels, with each reveal widening the conspiracy and raising the stakes. It’s strongest when it stays in pursuit mode; the middle section leans on information delivery more than surprise.

resonant_originality.reasoning: The premise feels like a recognizable thriller shape with a specific local skin rather than a truly singular engine. The custodian/podcast pairing and church-underbelly reveal are effective, but the story still reads as a variation on a known conspiracy template.

world_density_and_texture.reasoning: The high school, church, police department, podcast studio, and tunnel network create a coherent small-town ecosystem with institutional pressure baked in. The world feels story-generating because every location carries social power, secrecy, or surveillance.

tonal_specificity.reasoning: The script has a clear regional, blue-collar, late-night texture, and the contrast between Friday-night football energy and buried institutional rot is memorable. It stays in a sober thriller register rather than trying to overstyle the material, which gives it a grounded identity.

latent_depth_slow_burn_potential.reasoning: The church/police hierarchy and the rotating-chair idea suggest a larger system beyond the immediate case, which gives the story some depth. On the page, though, the conspiracy is still mostly presented as a plot engine rather than a layered social world.

relationship_density_and_ensemble_engine.reasoning: Ralph and Savannah carry the script well, and Daniels adds a useful pressure point, but the ensemble is still mostly functional around the central investigation. There’s enough friction for a feature, but not yet the kind of relationship web that generates endless secondary scenes.

lead_characters.name: Ralph Cipplone
lead_characters.demographics: Male, late 40s, working-class, white, local small-town resident.
lead_characters.hook: A quiet, methodical school custodian who sees what other people miss, Ralph is the emotional ballast of the story: observant, guarded, and carrying the weight of a past loss that makes him unusually sensitive to buried truth. He looks like a man who keeps his head down, but once he recognizes a pattern, he becomes relentless.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Bryan Cranston in Breaking Bad or Michael Keaton in Spotlight — a contained, layered adult lead whose stillness and moral pressure do the heavy lifting. It gives an actor the chance to play restraint, intelligence, and late-breaking resolve in a role that can quietly dominate the movie.

lead_characters.name: Savannah McMullen
lead_characters.hook: Savannah is the engine and the conscience of the investigation: sharp, skeptical, and unwilling to let a missing-girl case get filed away as routine. She has the confidence of someone used to being heard, but the script gives her enough vulnerability and urgency to feel personally invested rather than just professionally curious.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gave Jodie Comer in The Last Duel or Amy Adams in Sharp Objects a chance to control the room with intelligence and pressure. It offers a strong actor the chance to play drive, skepticism, and emotional escalation while staying in the center of a conspiracy.

lead_characters.name: Chief Daniels
lead_characters.demographics: Male, 50s-60s, police chief, local authority figure.
lead_characters.hook: Daniels is the story’s most useful ambiguity: a chief who knows more than he says, may be compromised, and keeps shifting between obstruction and reluctant cooperation. He reads as a man protecting a system he can no longer fully control.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of morally compromised authority role that lets an actor play pressure, concealment, and authority in the vein of Jeffrey Wright in The Batman or Shea Whigham in Boardwalk Empire. It’s a juicy supporting part because every scene can pivot on what he’s not saying.

lead_characters.name: Rick Tingling
lead_characters.demographics: Male, late 70s, elderly local power figure.
lead_characters.hook: Tingling is the polished face of the hidden machine: refined, composed, and chilling precisely because he treats the operation like administration. He’s not a cartoon villain; he’s the man who believes he’s preserving order.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is premium villain territory in the mode of Bryan Cox in Succession or Ben Kingsley in Sexy Beast — a role where calm authority is the menace. It gives an older actor a chance to play intelligence, control, and institutional rot with real presence.

lead_characters.name: Kayla Morris
lead_characters.hook: Kayla is the human proof that the conspiracy is real: frightened, trapped, and alive when the story finds her. She’s less a full arc than a crucial emotional and moral stake in the investigation.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that can be devastating in the tradition of the survivor parts in Prisoners or Room — brief on page, but loaded with emotional consequence. It gives a young actor a high-impact, high-stakes showcase in a pivotal rescue sequence.

technical.vfx_details: No meaningful VFX beyond basic cleanup and possible compositing for tunnel or crowd continuity.
technical.sfx_needs: Practical fight beats, car impact, door breach, flashlight-driven suspense, and police raid coverage.

platform_fit.series_engine_or_release_model: Feature release model; best positioned as a streaming-first or specialty theatrical thriller.

budget.note: Contemporary, interior-heavy, and largely practical: school, church, police, podcast studio, hospital, and tunnel spaces drive the schedule, with no VFX load and only modest stunt coverage.

casting.note: Ralph needs a very specific mix of quiet authority, grief, and late-breaking intensity, while Tingling needs an older actor who can play refined menace without tipping into caricature.

development.note: The conspiracy reveal is clear, but the script leans on familiar missing-girl / corrupt-institution beats, so the buyer conversation will center on whether the Skook-specific texture is enough to differentiate it.

audience_target.primary_audience: Adults who buy grounded conspiracy thrillers with moral stakes, especially viewers drawn to missing-person stories and institutional cover-up narratives.
audience_target.demographics: 35-64, slightly male-skewing but viable with women 35+; upscale adult audience that responds to prestige crime material.

budget_tier.note: Contemporary locations, modest cast, practical action, and no VFX keep this in the indie feature range.

types_of_buyers: indie producers seeking elevated crime material
director-driven buyers looking for a contained adult thriller
lane_fit.detail: This sits naturally in the adult, issue-adjacent thriller lane: serious tone, local specificity, and a conspiracy engine that can be sold on premise and performance. The church/police corruption angle gives it prestige gravity without requiring tentpole scale.

ip_potential.detail: Standalone feature: the Ralph/Savannah investigation resolves as a single case, and no secondary character is developed enough to anchor a separate spinoff.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The custodian lead is a real hook.
strengths.what_it_means: Ralph gives the movie an instantly legible, underused protagonist type that can attract actors looking for a grounded, blue-collar prestige role. That kind of part is attractive to buyers because it feels fresh without requiring a high-concept budget premium.
strengths.evidence: The opening hallway sequence and Ralph’s quiet observation of the school, followed by his line about the story starting after the clock hits zero.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The church-and-police conspiracy is easy to sell.
strengths.what_it_means: The premise gives the film a clean, high-stakes engine that buyers can understand in one sentence and market with urgency. That makes it especially attractive to streamer film teams and specialty distributors looking for adult suspense with a clear moral target.
strengths.evidence: The altered records, the church basement, the hidden tunnels, and the reveal that the operation runs through St. Andrew’s.

strengths.what_it_means: The Skook-specific football-night opening, church authority, and small-town institutional overlap create a world that feels lived-in rather than generic. That specificity helps the script stand out in a crowded thriller market and gives directors a clear visual and cultural identity to lean on.
strengths.evidence: The packed football field cold open, the podcast studio, the school archive, and the church basement/tunnel network.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The lead duo has clean chemistry potential.
strengths.what_it_means: Ralph and Savannah give the movie a strong two-hander dynamic even though the story is structurally anchored by Ralph. That helps casting conversations because the film can be sold as both a character piece and a suspense engine.
strengths.evidence: Their podcast banter, the shared investigation, and the hospital-room alignment after Ralph is attacked.

whats_special.headline: This is a contained, adult thriller with a strong blue-collar lead, a clean conspiracy engine, and a production footprint that stays inside indie-feature economics. The Skook setting and church/police corruption angle give it enough specificity to feel marketable to streamer film teams and specialty buyers looking for prestige crime material.

items.detail: The missing-girl-to-corrupt-church-to-corrupt-police progression is efficient, but it sits close to a well-worn thriller lane. Buyers will recognize the shape quickly, which means the script’s differentiation has to come from execution and setting rather than premise alone.

items.area: Savannah is more functional than singular.
items.detail: She drives the investigation and has clear competence, but the page gives Ralph the more distinctive inner life and observational texture. That creates a slight imbalance in the central duo, especially if the movie is pitched as a two-hander.

items.area: The middle section leans on exposition.
items.detail: Once the task force board, archive digging, and transfer-schedule reveals kick in, the script spends a lot of time explaining the system before the next physical turn. That’s not a fatal issue, but it does soften momentum in the stretch between the first discovery and the tunnel climax.

items.area: The supporting ensemble is thinly individualized.
items.detail: Daniels, Holmes, Gilbert, and Minadi all serve the investigation cleanly, but only Daniels gets a real moral wrinkle. For a feature, that’s enough to function, but it limits the relationship texture and reduces the number of scenes that can generate fresh energy outside the core plot.

issues.headline: The script’s main friction is not clarity — it’s familiarity. The buyer conversation will center on whether the Skook-specific texture, Ralph’s unusual lead profile, and the contained production footprint are enough to overcome a conspiracy-thriller shape that audiences will recognize immediately.
